name: Philippine Pangolin
description: The Philippine pangolin is endemic to Palawan and nearby islands. Covered in protective keratin scales, it curls into a ball when threatened and feeds almost exclusively on ants and termites using a long sticky tongue.
habitat: Lowland and mid-elevation forests, secondary growth, and agricultural edges across Palawan.
facts: Endemic to the Palawan faunal region — found nowhere else on Earth.
A single pangolin can eat tens of thousands of ants in one night.
Its scales are made of the same material as human fingernails.

name: Palawan Peacock-Pheasant
description: A stunning ground-dwelling bird endemic to Palawan. Males display iridescent blue-green ocelli on their plumage and perform elaborate courtship dances.
habitat: Primary and secondary lowland forests of Palawan.
diet: Seeds, fruits, insects, and small invertebrates
facts: The national bird of Palawan and a symbol of the province.
Males have metallic blue crests and peacock-like eye spots.
Katala Foundation works to protect its remaining forest habitat.

name: Palawan Hornbill
description: A large black-and-white hornbill found only in Palawan. It plays a vital role as a seed disperser, helping regenerate forest ecosystems.
habitat: Forest canopy from coastal lowlands to foothills.
facts: Pairs seal the female inside a tree cavity while she incubates eggs.
Their loud calls echo through Palawan's forests at dawn.
Critical seed dispersers for large-fruited forest trees.

name: Palawan Bearcat
description: Also known as the binturong, this arboreal mammal has a prehensile tail and a scent often compared to popcorn. The Palawan subspecies is smaller than its mainland relatives.
habitat: Tall forests with dense canopy cover across Palawan.
diet: Fruits (especially figs), small animals, and eggs
facts: One of the few mammals with a fully prehensile tail.
Their musk smells remarkably like buttered popcorn.
Mostly nocturnal and rarely seen in the wild.

name: Palawan Frogmouth
description: A master of camouflage, the Palawan frogmouth sits motionless on branches by day, resembling a broken stump. It hunts insects at night with a wide frog-like gape.
habitat: Forest edges, secondary growth, and wooded gardens.
facts: Nearly invisible during the day thanks to bark-like plumage.
Endemic to the Palawan group of islands.
Named for its broad, frog-like mouth used to scoop insects.

name: Blue-naped Parrot
description: A bright green parrot with a distinctive blue patch on the nape. Once common across the Philippines, wild populations have declined sharply due to trapping for the cage-bird trade.
habitat: Forest, mangroves, coconut plantations, and cultivated areas.
facts: Still relatively common in parts of Palawan compared to other islands.
Often seen in noisy flocks flying between fruiting trees.
Protected under Philippine wildlife law — trapping is illegal.

name: Crested Serpent Eagle
description: A medium-sized raptor of Palawan’s forests, often heard before it is seen. It specializes in snakes and lizards, scanning the canopy and forest floor from exposed perches.
habitat: Forest edges, secondary growth, and wooded hillsides.
facts: Named for its preference for snakes and other reptiles.
Distinctive whistling calls carry far across forest valleys.
A short crest of feathers rises when the bird is alert.

name: Mantanani Scops Owl
description: A small island scops owl found on Mantanani and other islets of the Sulu and Palawan region. Cryptic brown plumage helps it blend into bark and leaf litter by day.
habitat: Coastal forest, scrub, and coconut plantations on small islands.
facts: Restricted to a handful of small islands in the region.
Mostly nocturnal — day roosts are hard to spot.
Island populations are vulnerable to even small habitat losses.

name: Peregrine Falcon
description: One of the world’s fastest birds, the peregrine visits Palawan cliffs and coasts on migration and as a winter visitor. It stoops on flying prey at extraordinary speed.
habitat: Coastal cliffs, open forest edges, and rocky outcrops.
facts: Dive speeds can exceed 300 km/h in a hunting stoop.
A seasonal visitor and passage migrant in the Philippines.
Recovered globally after DDT bans in many countries.

name: Pied Imperial Pigeon
description: A striking black-and-white pigeon of coastal forests and small islands. Flocks move between fruiting trees, dispersing large seeds across the seascape.
habitat: Coastal forest, mangroves, and offshore islands.
facts: Bold pied plumage makes flocks easy to spot in flight.
Important seed dispersers for island forest trees.
Often nests in colonies on small islets.

name: Crested Goshawk
description: A forest hawk with barred underparts and a short crest. It hunts birds and small mammals through dense canopy, relying on surprise and agility.
habitat: Primary and secondary forest, wooded parks.
facts: Short rounded wings help it weave through dense branches.
Often perches quietly before launching a sudden chase.
Present year-round in suitable Palawan forest.

name: Grey-faced Buzzard
description: A migratory raptor that passes through and winters in the Philippines. Pale underparts and a greyish face help separate it from resident forest hawks.
habitat: Open woodland, forest edges, and agricultural mosaics.
diet: Frogs, lizards, insects, and small vertebrates
facts: A classic East Asian migrant that reaches Palawan each winter.
Often seen perched on poles or dead trees scanning for prey.
Flocks may move together on migration days.

name: White-bellied Sea Eagle
description: A large coastal eagle with a white belly and dark wings. It patrols shorelines and islands for fish and waterbirds, nesting in tall trees overlooking the sea.
habitat: Coasts, islands, estuaries, and large inland lakes.
facts: Adults show a clean white head and underparts.
Pairs often reuse the same huge stick nest for years.
A familiar sight along Palawan’s quieter shorelines.

name: Spotted Wood Owl
description: A large, boldly spotted owl of lowland forest and wooded gardens. Nocturnal hunters, they take rodents and large insects from perches in the mid-canopy.
habitat: Lowland forest, secondary growth, and wooded settlements.
facts: Round head without ear tufts distinguishes it from scops owls.
Deep hooting calls carry through still nights.
Day roosts are often in dense foliage close to the trunk.

name: Nicobar Pigeon
description: A iridescent green pigeon of small islands and coastal forest. Closely related to the extinct dodo’s lineage, it nests on offshore islets and forages on larger islands.
habitat: Small islands, coastal forest, and mangroves.
facts: Metallic green plumage shimmers in sunlight.
Often nests colonially on predator-free islets.
Populations are declining across much of its range.

name: Grey Imperial Pigeon
description: A soft-grey imperial pigeon of the Sulu and Palawan region. It depends on fruiting forest trees and is sensitive to hunting and habitat loss on small islands.
habitat: Lowland and coastal forest on islands.
facts: Restricted to a limited set of Philippine and nearby islands.
Quiet canopy bird — often detected by soft calls.
Seed dispersal helps maintain island forest diversity.

name: Palawan Leopard Cat
description: A small spotted wild cat endemic as a subspecies to Palawan. Camera traps often capture it along forest trails at night as it hunts rodents and birds.
habitat: Forest, secondary growth, and forest edges.
facts: Palawan hosts a distinct leopard-cat subspecies.
Mostly nocturnal and solitary.
Camera-trap surveys are key to monitoring its status.

name: Palawan Bearded Pig
description: A wild pig endemic to the Palawan faunal region, named for the pale beard of bristles around the snout. It roots through leaf litter and shapes understory plant communities.
habitat: Forest, secondary growth, and forest–farm edges.
diet: Roots, fruits, invertebrates, and plant matter
facts: Endemic to Palawan and nearby islands.
Important ecosystem engineers through soil disturbance.
Often recorded on camera traps along ridge trails.

name: Asian Small-clawed Otter
description: The world’s smallest otter species, found along Palawan’s streams, mangroves, and wetlands. Family groups hunt crabs and other aquatic prey with sensitive paws.
habitat: Rivers, mangroves, wetlands, and coastal waterways.
facts: Partially webbed feet with reduced claws for feeling prey.
Often lives in extended family groups.
Camera traps capture them on muddy forest floors near water.

name: Palawan Collared Mongoose
description: A slender forest mongoose of Palawan’s leaf litter. It forages for insects, small vertebrates, and fallen fruit along trails and stream banks.
habitat: Lowland and mid-elevation forest.
facts: Camera traps frequently record it on forest floors.
Active by day more often than many nocturnal carnivores.
Helps control insect and rodent populations.

name: Long-tailed Macaque
description: A familiar primate of Palawan’s forests and coastal edges. Troops forage for fruit and invertebrates and can become bold near human settlements.
habitat: Forest, mangroves, and forest edges near farms and coasts.
diet: Fruits, leaves, insects, and opportunistic foods
facts: Also called the crab-eating macaque.
Highly social — lives in multi-male, multi-female troops.
IUCN uplisted due to trade and habitat pressure.

name: Palawan Treeshrew
description: A small, squirrel-like endemic mammal of Palawan’s forests. Despite the name, treeshrews are not true shrews and are more closely related to primates.
habitat: Forest understory and secondary growth.
facts: Endemic to the Palawan faunal region.
Fast, nervous foragers of the forest floor and low branches.
Important insect predators in the understory.

name: Northern Palawan Tree Squirrel
description: A lively tree squirrel of northern Palawan forests. It races along trunks and branches, feeding on seeds and fruits high in the canopy.
habitat: Lowland and hill forest canopy.
facts: Endemic to northern Palawan.
Often heard before it is seen — sharp alarm calls.
Helps disperse seeds through the forest canopy.

name: Saltwater Crocodile
description: The world’s largest living reptile, found in Palawan’s rivers, mangroves, and coastal wetlands. Apex predators that shape aquatic food webs.
habitat: Rivers, mangroves, estuaries, and coastal wetlands.
facts: Can exceed 6 meters in exceptional individuals.
Tolerates both fresh and salt water.
Palawan still holds important wild populations.

name: Philippine Forest Turtle
description: A rare freshwater turtle with a distinctive pale band behind the eye. Once thought extinct, it survives in forest streams of Palawan and requires urgent protection from trade.
habitat: Forest streams, wetlands, and swamp forest.
facts: Rediscovered after decades without confirmed records.
Highly valued in the illegal pet trade.
Katala Foundation supports field conservation for this species.

name: Water Monitor
description: A large, alert monitor lizard of rivers, mangroves, and forest edges. It forages widely for carrion, eggs, and small animals, flicking its tongue to scent the trail.
habitat: Riversides, mangroves, forests, and village edges.
diet: Carrion, eggs, invertebrates, and small vertebrates
facts: Excellent swimmers — often seen near water.
Forked tongue samples scent molecules like a snake.
Common in many Palawan habitats but locally hunted.

name: Green Sea Turtle
description: A large marine turtle that nests on Palawan beaches and forages on seagrass beds and reefs. Adults are mostly herbivorous, grazing seagrass meadows that stabilize coastal waters.
habitat: Coastal waters, seagrass beds, coral reefs, and nesting beaches across Palawan.
diet: Seagrass and algae (adults); omnivorous as juveniles
facts: Named for the green fat beneath its shell, not its shell color.
Returns to natal beaches to nest after decades at sea.
Palawan’s pawikan nesting beaches are critical for Philippine populations.

name: Hawksbill Sea Turtle
description: A reef-associated sea turtle with a narrow, hawk-like beak used to feed on sponges. Its overlapping scutes once drove the tortoiseshell trade that pushed the species toward extinction.
habitat: Coral reefs, rocky coasts, and nesting beaches in the Palawan region.
facts: Overlapping shell scutes give the classic tortoiseshell pattern.
Critically endangered worldwide — still illegally traded.
Important grazers and sponge predators that help keep reef balance.

name: Bakawan Mangrove
description: A keystone mangrove of Palawan’s coasts and estuaries. Tangled stilt roots trap sediment, buffer storms, and create nursery habitat for fish, crabs, and birds.
habitat: Tidal mudflats, river mouths, and sheltered coastal lagoons across Palawan.
facts: Prop roots filter silt and protect shorelines from typhoon surge.
Juvenile fish and crabs use the root tangle as nursery cover.
Palawan’s mangrove belts are critical blue-carbon stores.

name: Narra
description: The Philippines’ national tree — prized for golden hardwood and cascades of yellow blossoms. Still found in lowland forests and planted avenues of Palawan.
habitat: Lowland forest, riverbanks, and open cultivated ground.
facts: National tree of the Philippines.
Flowers briefly carpet the ground in yellow after heavy rains.
Heartwood is durable and historically overharvested.

name: Palawan Pitcher Plant
description: A carnivorous pitcher plant of Palawan’s ultramafic and highland soils. Modified leaves form fluid-filled traps that digest insects where nutrients are scarce.
habitat: Ultramafic hills, mossy forest edges, and nutrient-poor clearings in Palawan.
diet: Photosynthesis plus insects trapped in pitchers
facts: Endemic to Palawan’s specialized soils.
Pitchers lure prey with nectar and color.
Highly sought by collectors — wild harvest is a threat.

name: Ipil
description: A heavy hardwood of coastal and lowland forests, once abundant in Palawan. Slow-growing and heavily logged for construction and boatbuilding.
habitat: Coastal forest, limestone woodland, and near-shore lowland forest.
facts: Timber is extremely dense and rot-resistant.
Often grows near mangroves and beach forest.
Regeneration is slow — recovery needs decades.

name: Talisay
description: A familiar beach-forest tree with broad, layered leaves that turn red before falling. Common along Palawan shores, providing shade and coastal wildlife cover.
habitat: Beaches, coastal strands, and nearshore villages.
facts: Leaves change color seasonally — a rare tropical deciduous display.
Fruits drift on ocean currents, helping the species colonize islands.
Shade tree for nesting shorebirds and resting travelers.

name: Palawan Cycad
description: Ancient seed plants of Palawan’s forests and rocky slopes. Cycads look palm-like but are unrelated — living fossils that predate flowering plants.
habitat: Forest understory, limestone outcrops, and dry hillsides.
facts: Among the oldest seed-plant lineages still alive.
Seeds and leaves are toxic if mishandled.
Slow growth makes wild populations vulnerable to harvest.
